title: Hundreds, tens and ones
goal: Read, count, write and explain numbers through 999.
look: The friends label a pretend library inventory. Why is the zero in 406 important?
learn: The places in a three-digit number are hundreds, tens and ones. 10 ones = 1 ten; 10 tens = 1 hundred. Count to 999 with these places.
worked: 406 = 400 + 0 + 6: four hundreds, no tens, six ones. 999 = 900 + 90 + 9.
play: Make a hundreds-tens-ones mat. Use paper bundles to show numbers named by a partner. Include numbers with zero.
hint: Inventory data are fictional. Zero holds an empty place.

questions.prompt: Write six hundred and thirty-two in digits.
What is the value of 7 in 374?

questions.answer: 305 has zero tens and five ones; 350 has five tens and zero ones.

title: Compare and order
goal: Order three-digit numbers using < and >.
look: Amina compares team totals. Which place should she compare first?
learn: Compare hundreds, then tens if needed, then ones. The sign < means less than; > means greater than. The open end faces the greater value.
worked: 427 > 398 because 4 hundreds exceed 3 hundreds. 452 < 459 because hundreds and tens match but 2 ones are fewer than 9.
play: Build three numbers from digit cards. Order them with comparison cards. Tell a story where number ordering helps.
hint: Read comparisons aloud in both directions. Use place-value reasoning.

questions.prompt: Give one use of ordering numbers.
questions.answer: For example finding the largest stock total.

title: Name equal parts
goal: Read fractions of shapes and collections.
look: Zainab divides a strip equally. What does each number in a fraction tell us?
learn: In 1/3, denominator 3 counts equal parts in the whole; numerator 1 counts selected parts. Use halves, thirds, quarters, fifths and sixths.
worked: One fifth of 10 tops: share into 5 equal groups, giving 2 each. One fifth is 2. Four sixths means select 4 of 6 equal parts.
play: Fold marked strips into 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 equal sections. Label a selected part. Use sets that divide equally.
hint: Use equal-sized wholes. Parts must have equal amounts.

questions.prompt: In 2/5, how many parts make the whole?
In 3/4, how many parts are selected?
Draw 5 equal parts and shade 2. Name the fraction.
Why are unequal pieces unsuitable for thirds?

title: Equivalent and ordered fractions
goal: Recognise equivalent fractions and compare fractions.
look: Musa folds equal-sized paper into halves and quarters. Can different fraction names show the same amount?
learn: Equivalent fractions represent equal amounts of the same whole. One half equals two quarters. With equal denominators, more parts means more amount. For unit fractions, more equal parts in a whole means smaller pieces.
worked: 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6. Also 1/3 > 1/6 and 3/5 > 2/5. Compare equal-sized wholes.
play: Overlay equal-length folded strips. Two quarters cover a half. Compare thirds with sixths using the same whole.
hint: Always identify the whole. Half a large sheet may exceed half a small one.

questions.prompt: Why is 1/3 greater than 1/6 of the same whole?
questions.answer: Three equal parts are larger individually than six equal parts.

title: Add three-digit numbers
goal: Add with regrouping and add three amounts in stages.
look: Daniel counts reusable paper sheets. How can an estimate help check his total?
learn: Align place values. Add ones, exchange ten ones for a ten if needed. Add tens, exchange ten tens for a hundred if needed. Add hundreds. Add three amounts in stages.
worked: 268 + 157: 8 + 7 = 15 ones, write 5 and exchange 1 ten. Tens: 6 + 5 + 1 = 12, write 2 and exchange 1 hundred. Hundreds: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. Total 425.
play: Build a sum on a place-value mat. Record exchanges. A partner checks by subtracting an addend from the total.
hint: Warm up with two-digit regrouping. Explain every exchange.

title: Add fractions
goal: Add fractions with the same denominator.
look: Amina shades equal parts in two colours. How can she name the total?
learn: When denominators match, parts have the same size. Add numerators and keep the denominator. Do not add denominators. Keep the same whole.
worked: 1/5 + 2/5 = 3/5. One fifth and two fifths make three fifths. 1/4 + 3/4 = 4/4 = 1 whole.
play: Divide a strip into six equal parts. Shade 1 blue and 3 green, without overlap. Total 4/6; show it is also 2/3.
hint: Model selected parts without overlap for addition inside one whole.

questions.answer: Part size stays the same; the count of parts changes.

title: Subtract three-digit numbers
goal: Subtract with exchanges and in stages.
look: Musa uses sheets from a stock. What stays the same when he exchanges a hundred for ten tens?
learn: Keep the total value unchanged in exchanges. Subtract ones, tens, then hundreds. If a story removes two amounts, remove the first and then the second.
worked: 432 − 178: exchange a ten to get 12 ones and 2 tens. 12 − 8 = 4. Exchange a hundred to get 12 tens and 3 hundreds. 12 − 7 = 5; 3 − 1 = 2. Answer 254.
play: Build 325. Remove 146 with place-value pieces. Check remaining 179 by adding 179 + 146.
hint: With zero tens, show both exchanges explicitly.

title: Subtract fractions
goal: Subtract fractions with the same denominator.
look: Zainab shades five sixths then erases two sixths. How much stays shaded?
learn: With like denominators, subtract numerators and keep the denominator. Equal-part size stays the same. Check using addition.
play: Fold a strip into equal parts. Shade some and cross out a few shaded parts. Write and check the subtraction.
hint: The whole strip keeps the same number of equal parts after selected parts are removed.

title: Multiplication facts to nine
goal: Build and recall facts through 9 × 9.
look: Daniel makes a dot array. What happens when he turns it?
learn: Turning a 3-by-4 array makes 4-by-3; both contain 12. Use known facts to build others. Practise every fact in the 1-to-9 table on the reference page.
play: Choose a fact from the reference table. Build it with counters, cover the answer, say it and check. Swap factors to see the same total.
hint: Use patterns and objects before recall. Speed alone is not understanding.

questions.answer: Turning the array swaps rows and columns but preserves 27 dots.

title: Multiply larger amounts
goal: Multiply two digits by one digit and three one-digit factors.
look: Amina puts 24 paper squares in each of three envelopes. How could splitting 24 help?
learn: Split a two-digit number into tens and ones. Multiply each part and add products. With three one-digit factors, multiply two first, then the third.
play: Build three groups of 12 with bundles and loose strips. Record tens and ones products, then combine. Try four groups of three pairs.
hint: Explain grouping with objects before a compact written algorithm.

questions.prompt: Four teams need 15 cards each. Total?

title: Share and group to divide
goal: Divide exact totals up to 48 by 2 to 6.
look: Musa shares 24 tops among four teams. Is he finding group size or number of groups?
learn: Division shares equally or counts equal groups. The sign ÷ means divided by. Multiplication undoes exact division. Here no objects are left over.
worked: 24 ÷ 4 = 6. Sharing among 4 teams gives 6 each. Grouping 24 into fours gives 6 groups. Check 4 × 6 = 24.
play: Use 12, 24 or 36 counters. Choose 2, 3, 4 or 6 groups that divide exactly. Share, record and check.
hint: Ask which quantity the answer describes. Assessed totals are at most 48 with divisors 2–6.

questions.prompt: Share 32 tops among 4 teams. How many each?

title: Factors and multiples
goal: Find factors, missing factors and multiples.
look: Zainab arranges 12 counters in rows. Which row sizes leave none over?
learn: A factor divides a whole number exactly. Factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. A multiple is a number multiplied by a whole number. First positive multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16.
worked: 3 × __ = 18 has missing factor 6. Correct factor pairs of 30 include 1 × 30, 2 × 15, 3 × 10 and 5 × 6.
play: Make all rectangular arrays for 12 counters. Record factor pairs. Count the first five positive multiples of 3.
hint: The legacy text has an incorrect factor example for 30. Use checked products here.

questions.prompt: Factor or multiple of 6: what is the difference?
questions.answer: A factor divides 6 exactly; a multiple is 6 times a whole number.

title: Balance the number sentence
goal: Find unknowns using relationships between operations.
look: Daniel makes both sides of a sentence equal. Can the blank come before equals?
learn: Both sides must have the same value. Addition undoes subtraction; multiplication undoes exact division. Use an inverse operation and substitute to check.
play: Write true sentences, replace a number with a blank, and swap puzzles. Explain a related addition/subtraction pair with an everyday story.
hint: Encourage several strategies. A repeated unknown in one equation keeps the same value.

title: Money calculations
goal: Exchange, add, subtract and multiply money values to ₦20.
look: Amina checks pretend receipts. What should a correct receipt show?
learn: These historical curriculum amounts are pretend exercises. Add costs, subtract for change and multiply equal costs. Read each card’s value. These are not actual market prices.
worked: Four pretend items at ₦3 each cost 4 × ₦3 = ₦12. Pay ₦20: change ₦8. Check ₦12 + ₦8 = ₦20.
play: Use paper value cards in shop role-play. Write count, unit cost, total, payment and change. Exchange equivalent values with partners.
hint: Keep products at or below ₦20. Genuine denomination examples need supervising adult verification.

questions.prompt: Check change of ₦5 after paying ₦20 for ₦15.

title: Measure lengths accurately
goal: Measure dimensions in cm/m and explain standard units.
look: Musa measures a garden label. Where must the ruler’s zero go?
learn: Length, width and height are dimensions. Place zero at one end and read the other end. Use a tape or metre stick for longer distances. Body units vary; standard units allow fair comparisons.
worked: A strip from 0 cm to 8 cm is 8 cm long. A strip from 2 cm to 9 cm is 9 − 2 = 7 cm long.
play: Measure a book’s length and width with a real ruler. Repeat in hand spans. Explain why standard results should agree more closely. Find another use for a measured length.
hint: The schematic ruler is not actual size. Use a physical ruler and its zero mark.

questions.prompt: Strip from 0 cm to 12 cm: length?
Strip from 3 cm to 11 cm: length?
Choose a convenient unit for door height.
questions.answer: m; cm also valid if accurately used.

questions.prompt: Measure your book’s length and width.
questions.answer: Two plausible readings with cm units.

questions.prompt: Why do standard units help comparisons?
questions.answer: Their size is agreed and does not vary by person.

title: Distance around the edge
goal: Measure and calculate perimeters.
look: Zainab puts string around a paper garden plan. What length is needed?
learn: Perimeter is the distance all around a shape. Add every outside side once using the same unit. Opposite sides of a rectangle are equal.
worked: A rectangle 6 cm long and 4 cm wide has perimeter 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 20 cm. A square of side 3 m has perimeter 12 m.
play: Trace a book cover. Measure and add all its outside sides. Check with string, then straighten and measure it. Discuss a frame or garden boundary.
hint: Perimeter is length, not area. Use cm or m rather than square units.

questions.prompt: Give one everyday use of perimeter.
questions.answer: For example measuring edging, a boundary or a frame.

questions.prompt: Why is 6 + 4 not the 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle’s perimeter?
questions.answer: It counts only two sides; all four total 20 cm.

title: Hours and minutes
goal: Read minutes and calculate simple intervals.
look: Daniel times an activity. How many minutes make an hour?
learn: 1 hour = 60 minutes. On an analogue clock each number step is 5 minutes. The minute hand at 3 means 15 past; at 6, 30; at 9, 45. The hour hand moves gradually.
worked: At 2:15 the minute hand is at 3; the hour hand is just past 2. From 2:10 to 2:35 is 25 minutes.
play: Show 1:05, 1:20 and 1:45 on a paper clock. Name a use of time measurement in cooking, travel or school.
hint: Start with same-hour intervals, then cross an hour on a number line.

questions.prompt: Write quarter past five in digits.
At 4:45 where is the minute hand?
Why is the hour hand between 3 and 4 at 3:30?
questions.answer: Half the hour has passed; it has moved halfway to 4.

title: Read a calendar
goal: Read calendar dates and explain their usefulness.
look: Amina marks a class event on a practice calendar. How does a date differ from a weekday?
learn: A full date gives a day number, month and year. Weekdays repeat every seven days. Read the calendar heading first. Months have different lengths.
worked: Our fictional practice month has 30 days and starts on Monday. Day 1 is Monday, as are days 8 and 15.
play: Make the practice month with Monday-to-Sunday columns. Fill days 1 to 30. Circle event dates. Explain why a real calendar helps plan appointments.
hint: Use an actual calendar for real event dates. Our diagram is deliberately fictional.

questions.prompt: One week after day 9: day number?
How many days in two weeks?
What three pieces make a full date?
Why check the calendar month and year?
questions.answer: The same date number can have different weekdays in different months and years.

title: Grams and kilograms
goal: Measure, compare and use grams and kilograms.
look: Musa checks a scale beside a grain bag. Which unit must he look for?
learn: Everyday weight measurements use grams (g) and kilograms (kg). 1 kg = 1,000 g. Check the scale starts at zero and read its unit. Scientifically these units measure mass.
worked: 2 kg = 2,000 g. A 700 g object is heavier than a 500 g object by 200 g.
play: With an adult, weigh safe small objects, including smooth stones. Record readings and units. Discuss why agreed units help buyers and sellers.
hint: No unknown minerals, dusty samples or heavy loads. Do not infer mineral identity by appearance.

questions.prompt: Stones of 250 g and 400 g: total?
Why agree a unit in a transaction?
questions.answer: Buyer and seller understand the same measured amount.

title: Measure in litres
goal: Measure liquids accurately in litres.
look: Zainab fills a measuring jug for the garden. Where should her eyes be?
learn: Litre, written L, is a standard unit for capacity and liquid volume. Place a graduated jug on a level surface. Read the liquid at eye height. Fill carefully to the mark.
worked: 3 L and 5 L total 8 L; the second is 2 L more. Half a litre plus half a litre makes 1 L.
play: With adult help, measure into a bucket using a marked 1 L container. Record litres up to a safe mark. Prevent spills and use clean water.
hint: Use plastic equipment. Do not taste liquids. Marks, not picture size, determine volume.

questions.prompt: Unit for bucket capacity: L or cm?

questions.answer: Set it level and read the marked liquid level at eye height.

title: Straight, curved and symmetrical
goal: Recognise lines and find lines of symmetry.
look: Daniel folds a paper shape. When do both halves fit exactly?
learn: A straight line does not bend; a curve bends. A line of symmetry makes mirror halves that match on folding. Check the whole outline, not just corners.
worked: A non-square rectangle has 2 symmetry lines. A square has 4: two through opposite side midpoints and two diagonals. Not every triangle is symmetrical.
play: Fold squares and non-square rectangles along possible mirror lines. Draw every line that works. Compare with an adult-cut scalene triangle.
hint: A non-square rectangle’s diagonal is not a symmetry line. A circle has infinitely many.

questions.prompt: How many in a non-square rectangle?
Draw one straight line and one curve.
questions.answer: An unbent line and a bending line.

questions.prompt: Draw a rectangle’s two symmetry lines.
Why does a non-square rectangle’s diagonal fail the fold test?
questions.answer: The folded halves do not coincide.

title: Draw and describe shapes
goal: Draw and compare squares, rectangles, triangles and circles.
look: Amina designs shape cards. Which properties remain when she turns them?
learn: Use a ruler for straight sides. A square has four equal sides and four right angles. A rectangle has opposite sides equal and four right angles. A triangle has three straight sides. A circle has no straight sides or corners.
worked: For a 4 cm by 2 cm rectangle: draw a 4 cm base, make right angles at each end, mark 2 cm sides, join the top endpoints. Check opposite sides.
play: Trace a round lid for a circle. Draw a square, a non-square rectangle and different triangles. Find approximate examples nearby.
hint: Test angles with a folded paper corner. Three curved sides do not make a triangle.

questions.prompt: Draw a square of side 3 cm.
questions.answer: Four 3 cm sides and four right angles.

questions.prompt: Draw a 5 cm by 2 cm rectangle.
questions.answer: Opposite sides 5 cm and 2 cm, four right angles.

questions.prompt: Draw a triangle; mark its corners.
questions.answer: Three straight sides, three marked vertices.

questions.prompt: Trace a circle; mark no corners.
How many right angles in a square?
Why does a turned rectangle keep its name?
questions.answer: Its side relationships and four right angles remain.

title: Read picture graphs
goal: Interpret horizontal and vertical pictograms.
look: Musa graphs invented game choices. What must be read before counting pictures?
learn: A pictogram uses pictures for counts. Read title, labels and key. Horizontal pictograms use rows across; vertical ones use columns upwards. Here each dot means one child.
worked: Practice counts: ball 4, skipping 3, clapping 2. Total 9. Ball has one more than skipping.
play: Read the graph with a partner. Rebuild it vertically with counters and the same key. Explain why totals stay the same.
hint: Other graphs can use a symbol for several items. Always read the key.

questions.prompt: How many more chose ball than clapping?

questions.answer: Heights 4, 3, 2; key one dot per child.
It gives the number represented by a symbol.

title: Make a graph and find the mode
goal: Collect, graph and interpret data; identify the mode.
look: Zainab wants to choose a class game fairly. What question could she ask?
learn: Collect one answer per participant. Group answers. Make a pictogram with a clear key. The mode is the category occurring most. Results describe only the people asked.
worked: Invented choices: ball, clapping, ball, skipping, clapping, ball. Ball 3, clapping 2, skipping 1. Ball is the mode.
play: Use invented data or a voluntary non-sensitive survey. Make a horizontal or vertical graph with title, labels and key. Check totals.
hint: Ties can produce several modal categories. Do not generalise a class survey to a whole town.

questions.prompt: What is the worked data’s mode?

questions.answer: Correct labelled graph; key one symbol per response.

questions.prompt: How many more ball than skipping choices?
Can two categories with 4 votes each both be modes?
questions.answer: Yes, if 4 is the highest count.

questions.prompt: Give a use of a class pictogram.
questions.answer: For example comparing choices to plan an activity.
